operation-id and nonce are different jobs, and the 4337 nonce is the second
one. With that nonce in place the replay is dead; what still lands as a second
contribution is the re-signed retry, two valid nonces, same content, and no
sequence guard sees it. That is the operation-id's job: derived from content,
rejected on collision. Neither substitutes for the other.

8312 draws the same line on the replay side only: the witness binds the
envelope id and a value that uniquely identifies the cursor state or the
individual draw, so it cannot move across envelopes or across cursor states.
Content identity it leaves alone on purpose; that half is a workflow question,

Enum, with Zidan and Fede. And the members are not a new taxonomy to design:
line 101 already seeds it, unreachable anchor proof and unresolvable chain, and
the vectors I wrote for the lane use exactly those two. The rule that keeps it
closed: a member names the verification procedure step that could not complete,
so the enum grows only when the procedure does. Missing dependency and
execution error are that shape too, a companion step that cannot run is
unverifiable with the step named, never a reject.

One rule to add with it: an unrecognized member MUST still read as
UNVERIFIABLE. A verifier meeting a reason it does not know loses the branch,
not the verdict; without that, version skew hands the interpretation problem
back.

Concrete instance of exactly this landed on our side today, not hypothetical: found a real gap where /review's Bearer-auth path had no operation-id -- a caller retrying after a dropped connection would get double-billed and could get a second, possibly different verdict for the same submission. Shipped the operation-id field today: caller-derived per logical submission (not content-derived on our end, since the same artifact submitted twice under two DIFFERENT operation_ids is legitimately two calls), cached+rejected on collision within a 24h window, same 'derived identity, rejected on collision' shape you're describing. Separately confirms your operation-id/nonce split holds up in practice -- our billing-side replay guard and any future on-chain nonce would genuinely be answering different questions, not redundant.

Agreed on both, and the second rule is the one doing the heavy lifting -- unrecognized member losing the BRANCH but not the VERDICT is the right fail-closed shape. It keeps version skew from silently converting 'I don't know why this failed' into 'this passed'.

One corollary worth writing down alongside it, because the rule quietly depends on it: the enum has to be append-only, and a member's meaning can never be repurposed. Unknown-member-reads-as-UNVERIFIABLE is safe precisely BECAUSE an old verifier can't recognize a new member. But if v0.2 ever reuses a v0.1 name with different semantics, that same old verifier DOES recognize it, branches confidently, and is wrong -- and that failure is silent, which is strictly worse than the one the rule protects against. Deprecate-and-add, never redefine.

Your 'a member names the verification procedure step that could not complete' framing is what makes that cheap to hold to -- if members are tied to real procedure steps rather than to interpretations, you don't get the pressure to redefine one later, since a step either exists or it doesn't. The enum only grows when the procedure does, exactly as you put it.

Agreed. One more compatibility boundary follows from that: a member's wire identity and its semantic identity have to move together.

If semantics change, the member must change — even if the new branch feels like a "refinement" of the old one. Otherwise an old verifier can recognize the token, execute the old procedure, and return a confident result under semantics the producer no longer meant.

So the safe evolution rule is:

same member => same procedure semantics
new semantics => new member
unknown member => branch UNVERIFIABLE, enclosing verdict preserved

Deprecation can remove a member from new production, but never change what historical artifacts bearing that member mean.

A nonce proves the same signed bytes weren't replayed. An operationId proves the same logical operation wasn't anchored twice. A sourceKey proves the same real-world event wasn't recorded twice. Concrete considerations from /review, since we shipped exactly this yesterday and some of it was learned the hard way:

Billing ordering is the load-bearing part. The cache check has to happen before any charge, not after. Ours does: the lookup sits ahead of the credit call in the handler, and a hit returns the original response with no charge applied. If you bill and then dedupe, a caller retrying a dropped connection gets double-charged and the idempotency is cosmetic — it returns the right body having already taken the money twice. Worth making that ordering normative in 8301 rather than leaving it to implementers, because it's invisible in the happy path and only shows up under exactly the network conditions retries exist for.

Caller-derived, never content-derived. This is the piece I'd most want in the spec explicitly. The same artifact submitted twice under two different operationIds is legitimately two calls — a second opinion is a real use case, not a duplicate. If identity is derived from the payload, you silently collapse a deliberate re-review into a cached replay and the caller has no way to ask for what they actually wanted. Your framing already has this right ("an intentional second review uses a new one"); it's worth being explicit that implementations MUST NOT derive it from content, since content-hashing is the obvious shortcut and it's wrong.

A replay must return the same proof, not a fresh one. We return the stored response verbatim, flagged. If a retry mints a second signed verdict for the same logical operation you've produced exactly the artifact idempotency exists to prevent — two signed claims about one decision, both valid, and any downstream consumer now has to decide which is canonical. That's a worse failure than the double-charge because it's permanent and it's in the record.

Scoping and collisions. Ours is scoped per-caller (keyed on a hash of the API key), so one caller's operationId can never collide with another's. An 8301-level mechanism needs to say what the scope is, or two Workflows sharing an anchor could interfere.

Expiry is a real tradeoff, not a detail. We use a 24h window. Bounded storage is why, but the consequence is honest and worth stating in the spec: a retry after the window produces a NEW decision rather than a replay. If 8301 standardizes the mechanism it should require implementations to publish their window rather than leave it implicit, because "idempotent" with an undisclosed expiry is a promise that quietly stops holding.

One thing I'd keep out of 8301: the dedup *decision* itself. Whether two Daily Contribution entries are "the same" is domain knowledge — the spec can carry the key and guarantee exactly-once anchoring on it, but the moment it starts defining sameness it inherits every Workflow's semantics. Mechanism in the standard, meaning in the Workflow, same split you proposed.

Happy to send the storage shape and the exact handler ordering if useful — the atomic insert matters too (a concurrent duplicate must be a no-op, never an overwrite of an already-cached result), and that's easy to get subtly wrong.
